sections.text: He who expects nothing, who is pure, watchful, indifferent, unruffled, and who renounces all initiative, such a one is My beloved.
यो न हृष्यति न द्वेष्टि न शोचति न काङ्क्षति।
He who is beyond joy and hate, who neither laments nor desires, to whom good and evil fortunes are the same, such a one is My beloved.
समः शत्रौ च मित्रे च तथा मानापमानयोः।

He who is alike to friend and foe, who is the same in honour and dishonour, in heat and cold, in pleasure and pain, who is free from attachment, who regards praise and blame equally, who is silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady of mind and full of devotion , that one is dear to Me.

Shri Purohit there is no comment on this sloka What is my purpose and destiny? We have been discussing chapter 12, Bhakti yoga, Yoga of Devotion. The first six chapters described karma Yoga -- the Yoga of action -- teaching us who we are as individuals, how our actions function, and how we can make our actions more efficient. We have seen two definitions of Yoga: Samatvam Yoga Uchyate and Yogah Karmasu Kaushalam.
The equanimity of mind is Yoga, and the dexterity in action is also Yoga. You can only be dexterous in your actions if your mind is quiet. That was the technique we learned in the first six chapters.
And at the end of those chapters we had Dhyana yoga, the Yoga of meditation. Bhagavan said, I consider a Yogi to be higher than even a Gnani, even a Tapasvi. So he said, You become a Yogi, Arjuna. Arjuna asked, How do I become a Yogi? He said, offer your mind and intellect to me, focus your mind and intellect on me, synchronize your mind and intellect with me, and you become a Yogi.
Bhagavan has defined the perfect Bhakta as the one who offers his mind and intellect and considers him to be the supreme goal. Now here we discussed that Bhagavan, the supreme self which is pervading everywhere, is the same self that you consider yourself. Right now I consider myself to be identified with this body, mind, and intellect.
Bhagavan said, when you tune your mind and intellect to me, align with me, and identify with me, you become my Bhakta. So thats the definition of Bhakta we learn upfront in this chapter: Mayy arpita manobuddhih -- one who has offered his mind and intellect to me. About it: in all our temples, the Bhagavans are standing there with the hand extended, hoping that some Bhakta will come someday and offer his mind and intellect. Ill fix it and give it back to him. But he says theyre all unemployed, because no Bhakta ever goes to offer his mind and intellect.
They go and offer coconuts and flowers and prasad, but nobody is interested in giving their mind or intellect to Bhagavan. So Bhagavan has defined in this chapter: the devotee is the one whose mind is fixed on him and whose intellect is aligned with him. We started this chapter with Arjunas question about the two types of Bhaktas: one who considers God to be manifested in a particular form and worships him as his goal, and one who considers God to be Nirakara -- without any attributes, only all-pervading.
Which one is better, which one is closer to him? And Bhagavan said, both are closer to me. But for somebody who considers himself to be embodied, who identifies with his body as himself, it is very difficult to focus on God without any attributes. Therefore, it is much easier for you, Arjuna, to focus on someone or something you consider as the representation of the supreme reality.
In this case, Bhagavan said, focus on me, Krishna, as the representation of the supreme reality -- see the entire divinity in that person.: just as we assign our entire patriotic feelings to the flag of our country. When that flag is raised in the stadium during the Olympic medal ceremony, all citizens of that country feel elated because that flag represents their entire identification with their country. Bhagavan said, in the same way, when you can see the entire supreme reality represented in one person or one form, then it is easier for you to worship through that one.
Then Bhagavan has given us choices: if you cannot offer your mind and intellect to me, at least do Abhyasa, constant practice. There are two ways to interpret this. One is to constantly keep trying to offer your mind and intellect to Bhagavan.
The other is to learn about the nature of God through the scriptures, so that you come to realize what the supreme reality is and then offer yourself to it. If even that is not possible, offer all your actions to me -- work for me. Surrender to me, and Ill take care of everything.
Its like when you work for a large company. Whatever you do in your position, youre actually doing it for the company. When you go to a meeting with your client, you dont say I am such and such. You say, I represent such and such company. The entire power of that company is behind you.
Nobody knows better than me, because I used to work for large companies. The last firm I worked at had 2,100 people. So when I represented myself as from that firm, they obviously knew I represented a 2,100-person firm.
When I left that firm and started my own, I had five people. When Id say Im NBG Architecture, first Id have to explain what NBG Architecture is, who owns it, and how it came into existence. Then Id say, Im the same person you used to meet. Because the power of that company is what youre representing.
The larger the company, the more power you have behind you. So if you identify with this limited mind and intellect, youre projecting the limited power of this mind and intellect. But if you identify with that universal mind and intellect, then when you work in the world outside, youre projecting the power of the supreme.
Bhagavan said, do all your actions for me. Consider me as your employer and then work in this world, and you will have the supreme power behind you to be successful in everything you do. If even that is not possible, then give up the anxiety for the fruits of your actions.
Karma Phala Tyaga -- that will give you peace instantaneously. All those other things may not give you peace instantaneously. But this one thing -- if you give up the anxiety for the fruits of actions -- will give you peace right away.
Na Chirat -- immediately you will get this peace. So therefore Bhagavan in the end said, Karma Phala Tyaga is the greatest devotion to me. In other words, you have given up the sense of ownership -- I am the doer and I control my destiny. Once you have given that up, all your anxiety will be gone and you will be aligned with me.
The greatest devotee is the one who gives up the anxiety for the fruits of actions. In the last few verses, from verse 13 onwards through verse 19, Bhagavan has been defining the perfect devotee, the perfect Bhakta. These qualities described for the perfect devotee are no different than the Muni we saw in chapter two.
The qualities are exactly the same, just presented in a different way. These are the very qualities for which Bhagavan considers such a person as his Bhakta. And these qualities into six categories.
After every verse, Bhagavan says Sa me Priyah -- such a devotee is closer to me, is dear to me. When he says dear to me, Bhagavan is not being partial -- if you have this quality, I like you; if you dont, I dont like you. Rather, that person is identifying much more closely with the supreme. The qualities we have been seeing from verse 13 onward start with Adveshta Sarvabhutanam Maitrah Karunayevacha -- he does not hate anyone in this world.
Now that is something we find very difficult, because we hate many things and many beings in this world. I hate cockroaches and I hate snakes. Bhagavan said, you may not want to associate with them, you may want to stay away from them, but you do not hate them. Its not like Parashurama saying, Im going to make this earth Nakshatri -- no Kshatriyas on this planet. You are not going to say, Ill make this earth without cockroaches -- because they have survived the longest. As we know, we will be gone, but they will still be there.
Bhagavan said, one who does not hate anyone -- and then we have seen several more qualities. And then we come to the verse: Yasmat na udvijate Lokah. This is a very important verse.
Lokat na udvijate cha yah -- one who is not disturbed by others, and who does not disturb the world outside. My behavior, my presence should not agitate others, nor should I be agitated by others. I used to work for a company.
I had moved to Dallas from another company, WZMH. They gave me a project and said there was already a project manager, but they were looking for a replacement. So they gave me that project.
I went to the first meeting and the contractor said, Rajan, Im glad that you are going to be the project manager now. The last project manager we had was a guy named Howard Johnson. He said, He may not say anything, he may not do anything, but as he walks into the room, everybody gets tense and agitated. Something about the way he handled people -- it just didnt make people comfortable. The contractor told me, you shouldnt be that type of person.
People should feel calm and comfortable in your presence. I remember another incident. My chief architect, where I was interning as a first-year architecture student, was the one who introduced me to the Vedantic teaching tradition.
He also took me to another saint, Sant Mota. He was somehow on a mission to introduce me to all great sages. I kept telling him, Padna, I have no interest in spirituality. But anyway, he introduced me to Sant Mota, who founded the Mauna Mandir.
His concept was that you stay alone in a room for as long as you can. People would sign up for one day, two days, one week, one month. The condition was that you just go there and do whatever you want to do -- chant, read Bhagavad Gita, read even a novel if you want to.
But you are not connected with the world outside. No phones, no newspapers. Take whatever books you want to take.
But other than that, you stay there. People used to come from all over the world to sign up for that Mauna Mandir. Im not sure whether its still there or not.
But he was called Sant Mota, and when Padna took me to him, somebody asked Mota a question. I was only 17 years old. I hear all about some being fake sadhus and some being genuine teachers. How do we differentiate between a fake guru and a real guru? He said, What I say is very simple. If you come to that person and you feel peace in your mind, he is a true Sadhu.
If in his presence you get agitated, consider him to be not right for you. I still remember that answer after all these years. It is such a profound statement. And Ill tell you what we experienced ourselves in the presence of Gurudev.
No matter how many questions you had, no matter how you went thinking, Im going to talk to and tell him that these people are doing this to me -- you go there, and you forget everything. You forgot what you were going to complain about. People used to just sit in front of for hours.
He would keep doing whatever he was doing. He was actually watching tennis in those days -- watch tennis because he was a tennis player. People would record all those Wimbledon matches, and when He was relaxing, he would watch tennis.
We will have like 15, 20 people just sitting there for hours without any words exchanged.

Anapekshah, free from expectations. This single quality from verse 16 strikes at the root of much human suffering. We have mortgaged our happiness, as the teaching says, to external conditions and other people. My children must perform well for me to be happy. My spouse must behave a certain way. My colleagues must recognize my worth. We have distributed the keys to our peace among countless others who may never use them as we wish. The true devotee, having identified with the inexhaustible Divine, becomes the reservoir of his happiness. This is not cold detachment but the deepest security, happiness that does not depend on the worlds cooperation.
Verse 17 describes one who neither laments nor desires (na socati na kankshati). This is freedom from the two movements that torment the mind: grief over the past and craving for the future. The devotee lives fully in the present moment, where the Divine actually dwells. Notice the phrase shubha-ashubha-parityagi, one who has renounced both good and bad fortune as defining experiences. This does not mean indifference to ethics but freedom from being psychologically tossed by favorable and unfavorable circumstances.
Verse 18 points to equanimity toward friend and foe, honor and dishonor, heat and cold, pleasure and pain. Practice this today with one pair of opposites. Choose something you typically react to strongly, perhaps praise and criticism. When either comes, pause before the automatic reaction. Notice the mind wanting to expand with praise or contract with criticism. Can you remain samah, even, in both? This is not suppression but observation. The goal is not to stop feeling but to stop being unconsciously driven by feeling. At days end, journal about what you noticed in these moments of attempted equanimity.
